Coi gigli e le vïole.meaning: violets (poetic diaeresis vïole scanning as three syllables)

Coi gigli e le vïole: Prepositional phrase opening the second strophe of Nannetta's fairy song. The archaic diaeresis in 'vïole' (vi-o-le) expands the word into three syllables to preserve the delicate ottonario meter.

scriviam dei nomi arcani,.meaning: let us write (1st plur. hortatory subjunctive, apocope of scriviamo)
some / of the (partitive preposition di + i)

scriviam dei nomi arcani,: Hortatory 1st person plural subjunctive ('scriviam') with poetic apocope for 'scriviamo'. Nannetta bids the disguised children to trace enchanted magical symbols in flowers.
dalle fatate mani: Prepositional ablative phrase of origin ('dalle fatate mani') dependent on 'germoglino'. The feminine noun 'mano' takes the irregular plural 'mani'.

germoglino parole..meaning: let sprout / may sprout (3rd plur. present subjunctive)

Inverted optative/hortatory subjunctive ('germoglino') with subject 'parole'. The fairy Queen envisions words blossoming organically from the touch of their fingertips.
Parole alluminate: Archaic past participle 'alluminate' (from medieval Italian alluminare, meaning to decorate manuscripts with miniature illuminations and gold leaf), evoking glowing magical script.

di puro argento e d'or,.meaning: of gold (preposition di + apocope of oro)

di puro argento e d'or,: Prepositional phrase modifying 'alluminate'. The poetic truncation 'd'or' (for 'd'oro') creates a crisp tronco rhyme with 'albor' and 'cacciator'.
carmi e malie. Le fate: Elevated classical noun 'carmi' (from Latin carmen) paired with 'malie' in apposition to the illuminated words, followed by the subject 'Le fate' of the subsequent sentence.
Idiomatic construction 'avere per cifre' (to possess as secret signs or letters). 'Fior' is the poetic truncated plural for 'fiori', acting as direct object.
Moviamo ad una ad una: Let us move one by one

Moviamo ad una ad una.meaning: let us move (1st plur. hortatory subjunctive / imperative)
one by one (feminine plural distributive idiom)

Moviamo ad una ad una: Hortatory 1st person plural 'Moviamo' (preserving the non-diphthongized Latin root) combined with the feminine distributive idiom 'ad una ad una' as the fairies glide in single file.

sotto il lunare albor,.meaning: glow / whiteness / pale radiance (apocope of albore)

sotto il lunare albor,: Atmospheric prepositional phrase setting the nocturnal scene. 'Albor' is an apocope of 'albore' (pale dawn light or soft moonlight).
verso la quercia bruna: Directional prepositional phrase leading the procession to Herne's Oak ('la quercia bruna'), where Falstaff lies cowering in terror.
Genitive phrase completing the reference to Herne the Hunter ('il nero cacciatore'), ending the lyrical section on an emphatic rhyming masculine monosyllable.
Alto là!: Traditional military sentry command ('alto là!'). Bardolfo feigns military vigilance as he pretends to stumble upon the prostrate knight in the dark.
Chi va là?: Pistola echoes Bardolfo with the standard sentry challenge ('chi va là?'), heightening the mock-terror for Falstaff.
Pietà!: Sir John's single-word plea for mercy, paralyzed face-down on the grass because superstition dictates that whoever gazes upon fairies dies.
C'è un uom!: Mrs. Quickly draws mock-horrified attention to the fallen intruder, using the existential 'c'è' and the poetic apocope 'uom'.
ALICE, MEG E NANNETTA: Libretto character heading marking the three Windsor women speaking and singing together in the masquerade.
Cornuto come un bue!: Ford's biting exclamation plays on the dual meaning of 'cornuto' (physically antlered and a cuckold), relishing the poetically just humiliation of his would-be rival.
Rotondo come un pomo!: Pistola adds his comic comparison, contrasting Sir John's spherical shape with the literary noun 'pomo' (apple/fruit).
Grosso come una nave!: Bardolfo completes the triad of similes with a naval metaphor, comparing Falstaff's colossal bulk to a galleon.
PISTOLA, BARDOLFO: Libretto character heading indicating Falstaff's two treacherous ex-followers taking command of the interrogation.

Alzati, olà!.meaning: get up / stand up (imperative alza + reflexive clitic ti)

Alzati, olà!: Reflexive imperative 'Alzati' with enclitic 'ti', accompanied by the stern commanding interjection 'olà'.

Portatemi una grue!.meaning: bring me (imperative 2nd plur. portate + indirect object clitic mi)

Portatemi una grue!: Imperative with enclitic pronoun 'Portatemi'. Falstaff delivers a classic comic quip, admitting that only a mechanical hoisting crane ('grue') could lift his ponderous mass.

Non posso..meaning: I can / I am able (1st sing. present)

Concise modal verb expressing absolute physical and emotional defeat, pinned to the earth by weight and fear.
Ford's observation carries double meaning: physically ponderous ('grave') and morally serious in his transgressions.
È corrotto!: Quickly initiates the mock-religious catechism, pronouncing Falstaff spiritually defiled.
È impuro!: The women chime in antiphonal chorus, declaring that the sacred fairy ground has been desecrated by an impure mortal.

Si faccia lo scongiuro!.meaning: let be made / let be performed (impersonal si + 3rd sing. present subjunctive of fare)

Si faccia lo scongiuro!: Passive/impersonal 'si' with subjunctive 'faccia' ('si faccia', let there be made). Bardolfo announces the ritual cleansing and exorcism of the intruder.
Alice whispers an aside to Nannetta, warning her that Ford's secret scheme to marry her to Caius is underway. 'Periglio' is the elevated poetic form of 'pericolo'.
Already Doctor Caius is looking for you.
Preverbal accusative pronoun 'ti' governed by 'cerca'. Alice alerts Nannetta to slip away before Dr. Caius can locate his promised bride in the dark.

Troviamo.meaning: let us find (1st plur. hortatory subjunctive / imperative)

Troviamo: Hortatory 1st person plural opening Nannetta and Fenton's coordinated evasion into the woods, completed in the following line.
Direct object of 'Troviamo', completing the rhyming couplet with 'periglio' (periglio / nascondiglio).
Then you will return quickly at my call.
Future tense 'tornerete' modified by the predicative adjective 'lesti' functioning adverbially. Mrs. Quickly will summon the lovers back for the surprise double wedding.
Spiritelli! Folletti!: Vocative plural diminutives rallied by Bardolfo to begin the mock-demonic punishment of Sir John.
Farfarelli! Vampiri! Agili insetti: Boito draws on Dante's Inferno (where Farfarello is a devil in canto XXI-XXII) and Gothic lore to build a mock-frightening catalogue of nocturnal tormentors.
del palude infernale! Punzecchiatelo!: of the infernal swamp! Prick him!

del palude infernale! Punzecchiatelo!.meaning: swamp / marsh (masculine in archaic poetic usage)
prick him / prod him (imperative 2nd plur. punzecchiate + clitic lo)

del palude infernale! Punzecchiatelo!: Frequentative verb 'punzecchiare' in the imperative plural with direct object clitic 'lo' ('Punzecchiatelo!'). 'Palude' is treated as masculine ('del palude') in poetic elevated style.

Orticheggiatelo!.meaning: sting him with nettles / whip him with nettles (imperative 2nd plur. orticheggiate + clitic lo)

Orticheggiatelo!: Inventive rare denominal verb 'orticheggiare' (from ortica, stinging nettle), commanding the spirits to scour Falstaff with nettles.

Martirizzatelo.meaning: martyr him / torture him (imperative 2nd plur. martirizzate + clitic lo)

Martirizzatelo: Imperative plural with attached direct object enclitic 'lo', completing the trio of dactylic commands ('Punzecchiatelo / Orticheggiatelo / Martirizzatelo').
coi grifi aguzzi!: Prepositional phrase describing the grotesque masks worn by the children. 'Grifo' evokes the bestial snout of a boar or demonic imp.
Accorrono velocissimi alcuni ragazzi ves: Some boys dressed as goblins run up very swiftly,

Accorrono velocissimi alcuni ragazzi ves.meaning: run up / rush up (3rd plur. present)

Accorrono velocissimi alcuni ragazzi ves: Stage direction describing the sudden onstage invasion of Windsor's masked children. The absolute superlative 'velocissimi' underscores their frantic, darting agility.

e si scagliano su.meaning: hurl themselves / pounce (3rd plur. present reflexive)

e si scagliano su: Continuation of the stage direction with the reflexive motion verb 'scagliarsi' governing the preposition 'su'.
Proper name completing the object of the preposition 'su' in the stage direction.
Ahimè! tu puzzi: Falstaff's groan turns into comic sudden recognition: in the midst of 'demonic' torment, he gets a blast of Bardolfo's notoriously foul breath.
Simile playing etymologically on 'puzzi / puzzola'. Falstaff instinctively identifies the 'demon' towering over him as his drunken henchman.
FOLLETTI E DIAVOLI: Choral heading for the masked children and adults launching their kinetic assault on Sir John.

Ruzzola, ruzzola, ruzzola, ruzzola!.meaning: roll / tumble / roll down (2nd sing. imperative or 3rd sing. present)

Ruzzola, ruzzola, ruzzola, ruzzola!: Fourfold rhythmic repetition of 'ruzzolare' (to roll, tumble head over heels), mirroring the physical rolling of Falstaff's massive body back and forth.
Pizzica, pizzica,: Opening refrain of Boito's sparkling Pizzica Chorus, adapting the fairy torment from Shakespeare's Merry Wives of Windsor into lightning-fast Italian octosyllables.
pizzica, stuzzica,: Rhyming paired imperatives ('pizzica, stuzzica') setting up a playful, relentless staccato rhythm.

spizzica, spizzica,.meaning: nibble / pinch off bit by bit (2nd sing. imperative)

spizzica, spizzica,: Iterative frequentative verb 'spizzicare' (derived from pizzicare), conveying miniature bites and pinpoint pinches.

pungi, spilluzzica,.meaning: prick / sting (2nd sing. imperative of pungere)
pluck away / nibble in tiny morsels (2nd sing. imperative)

pungi, spilluzzica,: Compound rhythm with irregular imperative 'pungi' paired with 'spilluzzica' (frequentative of spilluzzicare), evoking relentless insect stings.
finch'egli abbai!: Conjunctive temporal clause with subjunctive 'abbai'. The tormentors vow to pinch Falstaff until he howls like a beaten hound.
Ahi! Ahi! Ahi! Ahi!: Falstaff's four-beat comic yelps, puncturing the fairy chorus with genuine physical anguish.
FOLLETTI, DIAVOLI: Character heading marking the full goblin ensemble taking up noisy percussion and dances.

Scrolliam crepitacoli,.meaning: let us shake (1st plur. hortatory subjunctive, apocope of scrolliamo)

Scrolliam crepitacoli,: Hortatory 1st person plural 'Scrolliam' with classical noun 'crepitacoli' (Latin crepitaculum), referring to antique wooden rattles and clappers.
scarandole e nacchere!: Rare antique dialectal noun 'scarandole' (cog rattles/noisemakers) alongside 'nacchere' (castanets), creating an overwhelming acoustic assault.
Di schizzi e di zacchere: Prepositional phrase of instrument. 'Zacchera' is an evocative Tuscan term for flecks of wet mud or mire kicked up from the road.

quell'otre si macoli..meaning: wineskin / leather flask (metaphor for a bloated drunkard)
let be stained / bruised / dirtied (3rd sing. present subjunctive)

Passive/reflexive subjunctive 'si macoli' (from macolare/maculare, to stain or bruise). Falstaff's belly is derisively termed an 'otre' (wineskin).

Meniam scorribandole,.meaning: let us lead / conduct / strike (1st plur. hortatory subjunctive)
frolicking raids / playful skirmishes (diminutive of scorribanda)

Meniam scorribandole,: Verb 'menare' governing the playful diminutive 'scorribandole' (from scorribanda, a fast cavalry raid or incursion), applied to children running circles.

danziamo la tresca,.meaning: let us dance (1st plur. hortatory subjunctive / imperative)

danziamo la tresca,: 'Tresca' denotes a medieval frenzied peasant round-dance, characterized by energetic leaping and foot-stamping.

treschiam le farandole.meaning: let us dance wildly / romp (1st plur. hortatory subjunctive, apocope of treschiamo)

treschiam le farandole: Cognate accusative with the verb 'trescare' governing 'farandole' (the lively Provençal chain dance), illustrating the whirling ring of tormentors.

sull'ampia ventresca..meaning: on the / upon the (articulated preposition su + la)

Prepositional phrase setting the dance floor directly atop Falstaff's stomach. 'Ventresca' (cured pork belly) is a brutally comic butchers' term.
Zanzare ed assilli,: Vocative invocation of pestilential insects. 'Assillo' is the bloodthirsty botfly or gadfly, used in Italian for relentless torment.
volate alla lizza: Chivalric tournament terminology: 'scendere alla lizza' means entering the jousting arena, mockingly elevating the pinch-mob to knightly combat.
coi dardi e gli spilli!: Prepositional phrase identifying the weapons: miniature stingers ('dardi') and needles ('spilli').
Ch'ei crepi di stizza!: Optative subjunctive clause ('Ch'ei crepi', may he burst/croak). 'Crepare di stizza' is a visceral colloquial idiom for choking in helpless fury.

pungi, spilluzzica.meaning: pluck away / nibble in tiny morsels (2nd sing. imperative)

pungi, spilluzzica: Rhythmic return of the female refrain, sung in hushed staccato over the swirling orchestral figures.
ALICE, MEG, QUICKLY E FATE: Character heading indicating the female ensemble intensifying the rhythmic incantation.

Cozzalo, aizzalo.meaning: butt him / ram him (imperative cozza + clitic lo)
egg him on / incite him / provoke him (imperative aizza + clitic lo)

Cozzalo, aizzalo: Dactylic sdrucciolo imperatives with attached direct object enclitic 'lo'. 'Cozzare' refers to head-butting like a ram or horned buck.
dai piè al cocuzzolo!: from his feet to the crown of his head!

dai piè al cocuzzolo!.meaning: summit / top / crown of the head

dai piè al cocuzzolo!: Tuscan idiom denoting top to bottom ('dai piedi alla testa'). 'Cocuzzolo' humorously refers to the very peak of his antlered head.

Strozzalo, strizzalo!.meaning: choke him / throttle him (imperative strozza + clitic lo)
squeeze him / wring him out (imperative strizza + clitic lo)

Strozzalo, strizzalo!: Vigorous alliterative rhyming imperatives with enclitic 'lo', mimicking the choking and wringing of laundry.
Gli svampi l'uzzolo!: May his fancy vanish in smoke!

Gli svampi l'uzzolo!.meaning: vanish in smoke / evaporate / burn out (3rd sing. present subjunctive)

Gli svampi l'uzzolo!: Optative subjunctive with dative clitic 'gli'. 'Uzzolo' is a colorful vernacular term for an amorous whim or persistent itch, which must be smoked out.

Pizzica, pizzica, l'unghia rintuzzola!.meaning: blunt / turn back / wear down (2nd sing. imperative)

Pizzica, pizzica, l'unghia rintuzzola!: Imperative 'rintuzzola' (frequentative of rintuzzare, to blunt or turn the edge). The tormentors are urged to pinch so violently that their nails turn back on his tough hide.
DR. CAJUS E FORD: Character heading for Dr. Caius and Master Ford stepping up to lead the rhythmic masculine litany of insults.

Cialtron!.meaning: scoundrel / rascal / shameless buffoon (apocope of cialtrone)

Cialtron!: Truncated insult ('Cialtron' for 'cialtrone'). Boito begins a dazzling chain of masculine augmentative nouns in -on hurled like hammer blows.

Poltron!.meaning: coward / sluggard / lazy knave (apocope of poltrone)

Poltron!: Insult branding Falstaff cowardly and indolent ('Poltron' for 'poltrone'), rhyming with 'Cialtron'.
Ghiotton!: Insult targeting Sir John's bottomless gluttony ('Ghiotton' for 'ghiottone').
TUTTI GLI UOMINI: Choral heading marking the full male chorus joining the barrage of rhythmic insults.

Pancion!.meaning: big belly / potbelly (augmentative of pancia, apocope of pancione)

Pancion!: Augmentative of 'pancia' ('Pancion' for 'pancione'), directly assailing his gigantic belly.
Beon!: Agent noun from 'bere' ('Beon' for 'beone'), mocking his notorious appetite for wine and sack.
Briccon!: Classic Italian insult ('Briccon' for 'briccone'), completing the explosive succession of -on rhymes.

In ginocchion!.meaning: on bended knees / kneeling (apocope of in ginocchioni)

In ginocchion!: Adverbial posture idiom ('in ginocchion'), ordering the humiliated knight to prostrate himself like a penitent.
Pancia ritronfia!: Ford's insult pairs 'pancia' with 'ritronfia' (intensive of tronfio, bloated/puffed with self-importance).
Guancia rigonfia!: Alice's matching rhyming retort ('ritronfia / rigonfia'), mocking Falstaff's bloated, pendulous cheeks.
Sconquassaletti!: Inventive Italian compound noun (imperative verb stem 'sconquassa' + plural noun 'letti'), mocking the destructive impact of his weight in bed.
Spaccafarsetti!: Mrs. Quickly's compound noun ('spaccare' + 'farsetti'), deriding the corpulence that splits doublets at the seams.
Vuotabarili!: Pistola's compound noun ('vuotare' + 'barili'), scorning Falstaff's bottomless capacity to drain wine barrels.
Sfiancagiumenti!: Dr. Caius contributes a compound noun ('sfiancare', to exhaust/break the flanks + 'giumenti', packhorses/mares), evoking the poor horses crushed beneath Sir John.
Triplice mento!: Ford's anatomical jab highlighting Falstaff's folds of flesh, rhyming in -ento with the surrounding lines.

Di' che ti penti!.meaning: say / tell (2nd sing. imperative, apocope of dici)

Di' che ti penti!: The chorus demands a formal confession with imperative 'Di'' and subordinate reflexive clause 'che ti penti'.
Ahi! Ahi! mi pento!: Falstaff eagerly repeats 'mi pento' between yelps of pain, desperate to stop the pinching.
Uom frodolento!: Moral denunciation using the archaic Tuscan form 'frodolento' to fit the strict rhyme scheme in -ento.
GLI UOMINI: Libretto character heading marking the male chorus continuing their rhythmic catechism.
Uom turbolento!: Parallel noun phrase castigating Falstaff as a riotous disturber of public and domestic tranquility.

Capron!.meaning: he-goat / billy-goat / lustful old goat (apocope of caprone)

Capron!: Insult mocking both his antlered costume and his lascivious lechery ('Capron' for 'caprone', the quintessential symbol of lust).
Scroccon!: Noun derived from 'scroccare' ('Scroccon' for 'scroccone'), stigmatizing his habit of living at others' expense.
Spaccon!: Insult derived from 'spaccare' ('Spaccon' for 'spaccone'), targeting his bluster and tall tales.
Perdon!: Falstaff's breathless one-word cry for mercy, cleverly rhyming with the barrage of -on insults ('Perdon' for 'perdono').
Riforma la tua vita!: Bardolfo sanctimoniously preaches moral reform to his master, adopting the posture of a holy inquisitor.

Tu puti d'acquavita..meaning: you stink / reek (2nd sing. present of literary putire)

Falstaff unmasks Bardolfo by his breath alone. The verb 'putire' (to stink) governs the preposition 'di' ('d'acquavita'), rhyming hilariously with 'vita'.
LE DONNE: Choral heading for the women taking up the mock-liturgical litany over Falstaff.

Domine fallo casto!.meaning: make him (imperative fa + direct object clitic lo with syntactic doubling)

Domine fallo casto!: Mock-Latin ecclesiastical prayer: Latin vocative 'Domine' combined with Italian causative imperative 'fallo' (fa + lo, with raddoppiamento sintattico).

Ma salvagli l'addomine..meaning: save for him (imperative salva + indirect object clitic gli)
abdomen / belly (comic mock-Latinate form rhyming with Domine)

Boito's celebrated comedic invention: creating a pseudo-Latinized noun 'addomine' (from addome, abdomen/belly) to rhyme with liturgical 'Domine'.
Domine fallo guasto!: Continuation of the mock litany with causative 'fallo guasto' (make him ruined/wretched), rhyming with 'casto'.
Fallo punito domine!: Inverted litany with 'domine' at the cadence, praying for righteous punishment upon the sinner.
Fallo pentito domine!: Couplet completion with 'punito / pentito', pleading for Sir John's complete spiritual repentance.
Formal inquisitorial catechism: addressing Falstaff's spherical shape as a concentrated 'Globo d'impurità', demanding an admission of guilt.

Ben mi sta..meaning: it serves me right / I deserve it (idiomatic expression of resignation)

Colloquial Italian idiom of resignation ('Ben mi sta!'). Falstaff humbly admits his deserved punishment.
Second catechism challenge: 'Monte d'obesità' translates Shakespeare's 'this mountain of mummy' into Boito's grand mock-heroic verse.
Third catechism question: 'Otre di malvasia' evokes Prince Hal's insults of Falstaff as a vessel of wine and sweet Malmsey.

Così sia..meaning: so be it / amen (liturgical closing formula)

Liturgical closing formula 'Così sia' (the standard vernacular rendering of Latin 'Amen'), rhyming with 'malvasia' and concluding the mock-exorcism.
